sources.title: Influence of rapamycin on safety and healthspan metrics after one year: PEARL trial results
supports: one-year randomized human evidence for intermittent low-dose rapamycin
direct safety and healthspan measurements in adults interested in healthy aging
sources.limits: Does not establish lifespan extension or broad slowing of human aging. Several authors are affiliated with AgelessRx, so commercial conflicts and design limitations must remain visible.

sources.title: What is the clinical evidence to support off-label rapamycin therapy in healthy adults?
supports: review of low-dose rapamycin and rapalog evidence in healthy human adults
conclusion that human data have not established rapamycin as a proven therapy that delays aging in healthy older adults
sources.limits: A review rather than a definitive efficacy trial; the evidence base remains small and heterogeneous.

sources.title: Exercise and Weekly Sirolimus (Rapamycin) in Older Adults: RAPA-EX-01 Randomised, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial
sources.publisher: Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle (2026)
supports: 40 adults aged 65-85 randomized to 6 mg weekly sirolimus or placebo for 13 weeks alongside exercise
no improvement in the primary chair-stand outcome
99 total adverse events in the sirolimus arm versus 63 with placebo; one possibly drug-related pneumonia
sources.limits: Small exploratory study of short-term physical adaptation, not a trial of lifespan or major age-related morbidity. It cannot determine long-term longevity benefit.

sources.title: Rapamycin treatment for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias: a pilot phase 1 clinical trial
supports: eight-week open-label 1 mg/day rapamycin study in ten participants with mild cognitive impairment or early dementia
rapamycin was not detectable in cerebrospinal fluid after treatment
several Alzheimer disease and inflammatory biomarkers increased from baseline
sources.limits: Very small, uncontrolled, disease-specific phase 1 study. It is useful for target-engagement uncertainty, not as evidence about healthy aging efficacy.

sources.title: RAPAMUNE (sirolimus) prescribing information
supports: sirolimus is an FDA-approved drug for transplant-related indications
approved labeling does not include slowing normal human aging
sources.limits: The linked label is an FDA-hosted historical label and points readers to current FDA labeling; it establishes the regulatory indication boundary, not the current state of off-label prescribing.

sources.title: DNA methylation age of human tissues and cell types
sources.limits: Trained to predict chronological age, not health outcomes — a distinction from GrimAge, noted explicitly in the chapter.

sources.title: DNA methylation GrimAge strongly predicts lifespan and healthspan
supports: composite of methylation-based plasma-protein surrogates and smoking-exposure estimate
sources.limits: Trained on mortality data; predictive performance does not establish that changing the measured CpG pattern causes improved aging outcomes.

sources.title: Methodological literature on epigenetic clocks as causal vs. proxy biomarkers
supports: Mendelian-randomization evidence questioning whether clock CpG sites are causal aging drivers
distinction between predictive biomarkers and intervention targets
sources.limits: The causal interpretation of epigenetic clocks remains an active research area; this source should not be used to claim clocks have no biological value.

sources.title: The Biological Age Testing Market, From Research Promise To Clinical Reality
sources.limits: Secondary market overview. Company-specific scientific or clinical claims require direct verification from primary materials.
